title: Salt in the water
word: the whole five years in seven sits
hook: a father, a cup of salt water, and the line under year two: you are that
carry: tat tvam asi: the self in you is Brahman
tomorrow: year three: whose great story walks in next?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first look back: Ganesha is honored before every beginning, the path's first doorway. Today, the second look back.

A favorite song sounds different the first time it's heard on good headphones: a bass line, a second voice, a whole layer that was always there underneath. Year two of this path was that layer. After a year of first words and stories, it opened the texts underneath them: the big Upanishads, Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, the Ramayana read part by part. And the most famous lesson in all of it took nothing but a cup of salty water.
screen: `A LAYER UNDERNEATH.` → `YEAR TWO: THE TEXTS THEMSELVES.` → `A CUP OF SALT WATER.`

segments.voice: In the Chandogya, the sage Uddalaka has a son, Shvetaketu, who comes home after twelve years of study rather proud of himself. So his father gives him a lesson with no book. Put this salt in water, he says, and bring it to me in the morning. In the morning: where's the salt? The boy looks. It's gone. Sip from this edge, says the father. How is it? Salty. From the middle? Salty. From the far edge? Salty. You can't see it, the father says, but it's there in every drop. That finest essence is in all that is. That is the real. That is the self. And you are that, Shvetaketu. Tat tvam asi. This is the heart of the Upanishads: Brahman, the one reality, is in everything, and the self in you, the atman, is not apart from it. Year two found the same depth elsewhere: Patanjali defining yoga as the stilling of the mind's turnings, Valmiki's Ramayana read for itself. And this year, tat tvam asi came back as one of the four great sayings. Now this week, in one breath. Hear what is good. The power in your senses is Brahman's. Words match mind. The self is not the body. Teacher as god. Ganesha first. And: you are that.
screen: `SALT IN WATER, GONE FROM SIGHT.` · `SALTY IN EVERY SIP.` · `TAT TVAM ASI: YOU ARE THAT.` · then, large: `BRAHMAN IN EVERYTHING, AND IN YOU.`

segments.voice: If there's a glass of water near you, take one slow sip and remember Uddalaka's cup: the salt unseen, and in every drop. Then, if there's paper near you, write one line from this path that has stayed with you, in your own hand. Read it back slowly, once, and rest with it.
The second look back, to year two: the texts under the stories, and a father who taught his son with salt.
screen: `THE WHOLE FIVE YEARS IN SEVEN SITS — today's word`.

segments.voice: To carry: tat tvam asi, the self in you is Brahman. The salt is in every sip. That's the week.

screen: `DAY 1778 COUNTS.` → `THE SUMMIT OF THE RANGES · 2 OF 14.` → `TOMORROW: YEAR THREE. WHOSE STORY IS NEXT?`

fork.setup: your little cousin asks, 'if God is real, where is he? I can't see him.' which story from year two answers that?
options: Uddalaka's salt in water: unseen, yet in every sip. tat tvam asi.

fork.reveal: the salt can't be seen but is tasted everywhere. the Chandogya says that finest essence is in all things, and in you.

chat.meaning: In the Chandogya, Uddalaka shows Shvetaketu salt he can't see but tastes in every sip: that essence is in all things, and you are that. Hinduism holds many views; this is one of its most famous lines.

tie.story: Uddalaka dissolved salt in water and showed Shvetaketu it was in every sip, unseen: you are that.
tie.friend: Priya can give Sam one real line: in the Upanishads, Brahman is in everything and in every person, like the salt.
